items.output: My first time in the pool, the water seemed vast and unyielding, making my breath catch in my throat. With each stroke, I focused on rhythm and trust, letting my arms and legs find their own rhythm. My instructor’s steady guidance made all the difference, turning panic into purpose. After weeks of early mornings and sore muscles, I surprised myself by swimming across the shallow end without stopping. That moment—standing on the far wall, dripping and smiling—proved that courage isn’t the absence of fear, but the decision to move despite it.

items.prompt_text:
Write a short piece about learning to swim as an adult. Follow every rule below.

1. Begin with a markdown heading line of the form "# Title".
2. Do not use the word "felt" anywhere.
3. End the response with the exact phrase "More soon." and nothing after it.
4. Do not use any commas.

Output only the piece itself.
items.output:
# The First Stroke

The water shimmered under the morning sun as I approached the edge of the pool my toes curling over the concrete lip my breath catching in my throat. Adults often carry more fear into the water than children not because the water is more dangerous but because the mind remembers every stumble every misstep every moment of doubt. I stepped in slowly letting the coolness rise past my ankles my knees my waist. The world shifted as I submerged myself up to my shoulders the silence broken only by the gentle lap of waves against the side. My instructor waited patiently her voice steady and kind. Breathe she said. Tilt your head. Kick gently. I tried. I spluttered. I sank. I tried again. Each time I pushed off the wall my arms cutting through the surface my legs finding rhythm the water no longer an enemy but a partner. By the end of the week I floated on my back staring up at the sky my body weightless my mind quiet. Swimming is not just movement it is trust. Trust in the water trust in yourself. More soon.
